title: Analytics dimensions are explored top-down by setting a high level of detail and reading the available paths back before narrowing the select
content:
The analytics engine's dimensional model is hierarchical (paths like `atlas/scopes/SUP/I/PHOENIX/`), and the documented way to work with it is **general first, then narrow**:

> "Looking at the dimension section in the filter options: to see available sub paths for the budget, leave the `select: "atlas"` and `lod` as 5. With `lod: 5` you'll be able to see the different paths available under your defined filter. Then, later, you can apply a more detailed path in the `select: "atlas/..."` path that will suit your needs."

```json
{ "filter": { "dimensions": [ { "name": "budget", "select": "atlas", "lod": 5 } ] } }
```

So `lod` (level of detail) is an **exploration tool** as much as a rollup depth: a query is also how you discover the taxonomy. The same applies to the vocabulary itself — `analytics { metrics }` and `analytics { dimensions { name values { path label description icon } } }` are queries whose whole purpose is to tell you what you may filter on.

Two operational rules from the same page: **upper- and lower-case matter** for metric and granularity names, so a mistyped case returns nothing rather than erroring; and **fetch per specified path** if performance is a concern, rather than pulling a broad subtree.

The guidance on combining dimensions is judgement, not mechanism, and its useful half is the warning: combining dimensions adds depth, but "avoid overly complex combinations that might lead to confusing or inconclusive results."
